content: Generalized weakness refers to the inability to exert force with one’s muscles to a degree that would be expected based on the individual’s general physical fitness. This condition can arise from dysfunction in the muscles, nerves, or the neuromuscular junction. The causes of generalized weakness are diverse and may include cardiovascular, chemical, dermatologic, drug-related side effects, endocrine, environmental, gastrointestinal, genetic, hematologic, iatrogenic, infectious, musculoskeletal, neurologic, nutritional, oncologic, overdose-related, psychiatric, and renal factors. Strength testing is often employed during the diagnostic process for muscular disorders before the underlying cause is identified. In many cases, the cause of weakness can be determined through a detailed history and physical examination. Electromyography (EMG) can help identify the type of weakness, but in some instances, a muscle biopsy or additional laboratory tests may be required. Life-Threatening Causes Life-threatening causes of generalized weakness include conditions that, if untreated, may result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours. These include: Cadmium poisoning Dicamba poisoning Fluoride poisoning Hexane-2,5-dione poisoning Temik poisoning Benztropine Mesylate overdose Hypercalcemia Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis Hypermagnesemia Hypermethioninemia Hypokalemic periodic paralysis Hypomagnesemia Hypophosphatemia Uremia Common Causes Common causes of generalized weakness include: Guillain-Barré syndrome Myasthenia Gravis Polymyositis Lambert-Eaton syndrome Botulism Diagnosis The diagnostic process for generalized weakness often follows an algorithm based on the guidelines of the American Academy of Neurology. This involves a systematic approach to identifying the underlying cause. Treatment The primary treatment for generalized weakness is to address the underlying cause. Specific treatments for conditions such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, Myasthenia Gravis, Polymyositis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, and Botulism are available and should be tailored to the individual diagnosis. Do’s Confirm true muscle weakness during the physical examination and differentiate it from muscle pain or fatigue. Obtain a detailed social and family history to assess for potential genetic disorders. Review the patient’s medication list for possible drug-related causes. Look for signs of upper and lower motor neuron involvement. Assess whether the weakness is symmetrical or asymmetrical and identify any exacerbating factors. Order thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) testing. Test for glucose and vitamin B12 levels if a deficiency is suspected. Conduct serum and urine testing for drug and toxin exposure. Perform electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies if initial laboratory results are inconclusive. Don’ts Avoid using a muscle biopsy as the initial diagnostic test. This should generally be reserved for cases where all other diagnostic evaluations have failed to identify a cause.
